item.title: Book spells
item.description: Stanford Events — Boil, boil, toil and trouble… what bewitching book will you find at the Education Library? Our witchy book display has a little bit of magic for everyone! Meet witches who are mischievous, adventurous, and sometimes downright wicked. From little witches who aren’t too scary to cooking witches (spoiler alert the frog lives!) and skin shedding fireball witches for older readers, there’s plenty here to scare up a good read. So come to the Education Library, pick a book, and see if you can find a story that puts you under its spell! Location: Education (Cubberley Bldg)

item.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
item.description: Stanford Events — Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions. Institutional Seat (2022) modifies a standard bench from the museum’s galleries into a version that is more comfortable for all museum visitors. Surround Sound (2022) attends to the floor of the gallery with dance-floor materials. Over the course of the exhibition, this floor will collect marks made by visitors’ shoes, strollers, and wheelchair treads, like another form of tally or notation. Carolyn Laz

item.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
item.description: Stanford Events — Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery. From her elegant French gowns to a colossal painting of her jewels, from the Egyptian artifacts she acquired for her fledgling museum to a Hawaiian skirt she may or may not have purchased immediately before her suspicious death, Jane! presents various idiosyncratic artifacts of Stanford lore—many shown for the very first time, and very likely for the last. IMAGE: Napoleon T. Sarony, Portrait of Jane Lathrop Stanford, 1871. Photograph with charcoal touch up, 55 ½ x 45 in. Cantor Arts Center, Stanford University, Stanford Family Collections, JLS.18217 MUSEUM HOUR

item.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
item.description: Stanford Events — The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future. The exhibition explores Kim’s concept of “Indigenous Futures” through art as a form of civilizational transformation, expressing p'owŏl (포월 抱越), embracing and transcending the pain and contradictions of reality while reaching toward new possibilities for the future. The opening reception on October 8 will feature an artist talk and a Korean mask dance (탈춤 t'alch'um) performance by Kim Bong-Jun and Che Se-hyun, a Seattle-based creative director and multidisciplinary artist. item.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
item.description: Stanford Events — Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France. Though commercially unsuccessful, these experiments laid the groundwork for the scanning, machining, and printing technologies ubiquitous today. Bringing together these rare artifacts, the exhibition opens up a little-known chapter of history to reveal the roots and richness of our contemporary world. An accompanying catalogue features four newly commissioned essays accompanied by previously unpublished documentation,

item.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
item.description: Stanford Events — Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition. Location: Green Library, Bing Wing

item.description: Stanford Events — In this guided meditation, we’ll ground ourselves in basic mindfulness meditation to cultivate clarity, stability, concentration, and calm. From a more internally connected place we will use the power of our imagination to envision the world we want to live in. This inspiring meditation is based on the idea that if we want to see healthier, kinder, and more ethical social, political, and environmental systems worldwide, we have to start with imagining it. This practice also will address the sense of hopelessness and disempowerment. This iPause Practice is part of a two-part series with Diana Winston in the Contemplation By Design Summit. To deepen the skills you develop during this iPause Guided practice, please consider attending Diana Winston's keynote lecture titled Reclaiming Presence and Ethical Grounding in Challenging Times on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 4:00-5:15pm. item.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail
item.description: Stanford Events — Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century. The exhibition reveals the anachronistic and provocative juxtapositions of artworks in avant-garde magazines and books which created a radically new vision that would go on to influence television and the internet. Curated by Altair Brandon-Salmon. Bowes Art & Architecture Library hours: M-Th 9-7pm; Friday 9-5pm; Sunday 12-6pm. Tour by Dr. Brandon-Salmon on 9/5 at 6 pm prior to Electric Contrasts Study Evening. Location: McMurtry Building

item.title: Mine Less, Last Longer? Singapore Solutions for Critical Materials in Energy and Electronics
item.description: Stanford Events — Lithium, cobalt, gallium and the rare earth elements underpin both the energy transition and modern electronics, yet their supply chains are concentrated, carbon-intensive and increasingly shaped by geopolitics. For a resource-scarce city-state like Singapore that makes 1 in 10 of the world’s semiconductor chips, the question is less where to mine and more of how we keep critical materials in use for longer. Dr. Richard Dasher, Director of the US-ATMC, will moderate the session. About our speaker: Benjamin C. K. Tee is Professor of Materials Science and Engineering at the National University of Singapore (NUS) and Vice President (Ecosystem Building) at NUS, where he oversees innovation and startup ecosystem growth programs. He holds the NUS College of Design and Engineering Dean’s Chair and received his PhD in Electrical Engineering from Stanford University in 2014. item.description: Stanford Events — Join the 2026 Stanford Food Summit on Friday, October 23, 2026, from 8 AM to 5 PM at the Arrillaga Alumni Center. This in-person event will bring together faculty, researchers, staff, students, clinicians, and other members of the Stanford community working across food, health, sustainability, engineering, education, business, policy, and more. The Summit is designed to spark connections and collaboration across Stanford’s seven schools and two hospitals. Come discover the breadth of food-related work happening across Stanford, meet colleagues from across the university, and explore new opportunities to work together around the future of food at Stanford. Registration is required. The event will be Stanford-centered, with a limited number of external collaborators invited when their expertise or partnership can meaningfully contribute to the conversation. item.title: Steal This Story, Please!, Documentary screening w/Amy Goodman & Tia Lessin
item.description: Stanford Events — This compelling documentary poses a question: what happens to democracy when the press stops challenging power? Taking on politicians, CEOs and riot police, Amy Goodman, founder and host of Democracy Now!, the largest independent news organization in the US, has reported from on the ground some of the most urgent and underreported stories of our time. Steal This Story, Please! is a gripping account of this fearless and trailblazing journalist, whose unwavering commitment to truth-telling spans three decades of turbulent history. Drawing on an extraordinary archive, Academy Award-nominated filmmakers Carl Deal and Tia Lessin (Trouble the Water, Citizen Koch, The Janes) take us behind the scenes with the warm, wisecracking granddaughter of an Orthodox rabbi — raised in a tradition of asking hard questions — as she navigates a media landscape reshaped by technology, corporate consolidation, and fierce political assaults on the press. item.title: Ron Alexander Memorial Lectures in Musicology – Joy H. Calico, UCLA
item.description: Stanford Events — Title: A Theory of Operatic Scene Type Abstract: Scholars of opera since Salome - a placeholder for the historical moment at which one could no longer count on functional harmony, straightforward narrative, or tonally-defined forms at the opera - need ways to talk about opera that are not confined to the silos of composer, subgenre, and style, nor reduced to mere reportage. Inspired by Saariaho's L'amour de loin, I recognized that certain scenes have recurred over the centuries, presumably because they make for good theater and offer tantalizing opportunities for musical and poetic expression as well as virtuosic display: love duets, diegetic songs, rage arias. Each of these narrative nodes has accrued features pertaining to music, vocalism, poetry, character, performance practice, and/or staging, that, in the aggregate, constitute a scene type. item.title: 36th Annual Jonathan J. King Lecture: Dr. Bryant Lin & Dr. Shoshana Ungerleider
item.description: Stanford Events — The Girand Center for Biomedical Ethics is pleased to announce this year’s speaker, Dr. Bryant Lin, in conversation with Dr. Shoshana Ungerleider, for the 36th Annual Jonathan J. King Lecture. We invite you to join us on Thursday, November 5 at 5:30pm PT in the Cedar Room at the Stanford Faculty Club or via livestream for My Cancer Journey: Happiness and Sadness, Hope and Fear. In this talk, Dr. Lin will share a candid and deeply personal reflection on living with terminal cancer. As a leading researcher, cancer advocate, and patient, he brings a rare perspective to the realities of serious illness, clinical care, hope, and what it means to live fully in the face of uncertainty. Joining Dr. Lin is Dr. Shoshana Ungerleider, a physician, journalist, producer, and leading voice in compassionate, patient-centered care.
